newsitem.title: south africa: S.African defence minister to seek amnesty.
newsitem.headline: S.African defence minister to seek amnesty.

text.p: South African Defence Minister Joe Modise will seek an amnesty for his actions as a guerrilla leader, but two other controversial politicians have ruled out trying to make the December 14 deadline, their spokesmen said on Wednesday.

"He intends to do it before the deadline," Modise's spokesman Brigadier Kobus Botha said in a telephone interview. He declined to specify incidents for which Modise would accept personal responsibility.

But a spokesman for F.W. de Klerk, South Africa's last white president from 1989 to 1994, said he had no intention of applying to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission for indemnity from prosecution.
"He has already indicated that he acted within the law all the time and that therefore he sees no necessity to apply for amnesty," the spokesman said.
Winnie Mandela, divorced wife of President Nelson Mandela and an anti-apartheid activist in her own right, also had no intention of applying for amnesty, her spokesman Allan Reynolds told Reuters.

At the height of anti-government protests in the mid-1986 Mrs Mandela issued what appeared to be a public endorsement of "necklace" killings, in which township youths burned to death colleagues they suspected of collaborating with apartheid.
De Klerk's National Party has said those responsible for necklacings -- the placing of a burning tyre around a victim's neck -- should be hauled before the truth commission.
Modise is so far the only African National Congress cabinet minister to express his intention to seek amnesty for actions during the war against white minority rule.
Members of all political groups must apply for amnesty for human rights violations by December 14 or face the possibility of being prosecuted if evidence emerges against them.
Modise, who led the ANC's armed wing during much of the anti-apartheid struggle, first indicated in June he would apply but doubts later arose over whether the party regarded it as necessary.

Archbishop Desmond Tutu threatened to quit as chairman of the truth commission last month unless the ANC -- now the ruling party -- made clear it was not assuming the right to declare its members immune from prosecution.
The ANC gave Tutu an assurance it would encourage all members to apply for amnesty if they felt they might need it.
President Mandela first mooted the idea of a truth commission when reports emerged in the early 1990s of human rights abuses committed by ANC leaders against subordinates in guerrilla camps in exile.
Mandela said a probe into all human rights abuses during apartheid would ensure that the events in the camps were seen in their proper context.
Asked if Modise's amnesty application would cover abuses in the ANC camps, Botha said: "It will apply to all the activities."
The commission is intended to promote reconciliation between the forces that fought a bitter and often dirty war against each other after the ANC took up arms in 1960.
The ANC's political opponents have demanded it name those responsible for, among other things, bomb attacks that killed civilians in the 1980s.
